terms.definition: Money given on a regular schedule, often by a parent or guardian, that a young person can practice earning, spending, saving, or budgeting.
The yearly cost of borrowing money, including interest and certain fees, shown as a percentage.
A machine that lets you withdraw cash, deposit money, and check your balance using a debit or ATM card.
Insurance that helps cover certain costs after a vehicle accident, theft, or other covered loss. Coverage requirements and policy terms vary.
An account at a bank or credit union used to hold and manage money, such as a checking or savings account.
A federal legal process that may help a person or business address debts under court supervision. The effects depend on the type of case and the person's circumstances.
A plan for how income will be used for spending, saving, and debt payments during a set period.
A short-term financing option that splits a purchase into smaller payments over time. Missed payments can lead to fees.
A bank or credit union account designed for regular deposits, purchases, bill payments, transfers, and withdrawals.
Interest calculated on the original amount and on interest that has already been added. It can help savings grow or make debt cost more.
The ability to borrow money or receive goods or services now with an agreement to pay later, often with interest or fees.
A revolving credit account that lets you borrow up to a limit for purchases or other transactions. Interest and fees depend on the account terms and how the balance is repaid.
The maximum amount a lender allows you to borrow on a revolving account such as a credit card.
A record of credit accounts, payment history, balances, inquiries, and certain public-record information maintained by a consumer reporting company.
A number calculated from information in a credit report to estimate credit risk. Scoring models and number ranges vary.
Money or another financial obligation owed to a person, company, or government.
The amount you pay out of pocket on an insurance claim before your insurance starts paying.
Spending that is not required for basic needs or fixed obligations, such as entertainment or optional purchases.
Money set aside for unexpected expenses or a temporary loss of income.
A person who starts and operates a business and takes responsibility for its planning, costs, and risks.
Used to apply for federal grants, work-study funds, and student loans. States and schools may also use FAFSA information for aid decisions.
Charges for a service, transaction, account feature, late payment, or other activity.
Money that helps pay for college or career school, including grants, scholarships, work-study earnings, and student loans.
Expenses that are usually due on a regular schedule and stay fairly predictable, such as rent, insurance, or a phone plan.
A period when certain credit card purchases may avoid interest if the required balance is paid by the due date. Not every transaction or account has a grace period.
Financial aid that generally does not have to be repaid, although eligibility rules and other conditions may apply.
Income before taxes, benefits, and other deductions are taken out.
The cost of borrowing money, or the money earned on savings, usually shown as a yearly percentage rate.
A temporary work-based learning experience that may be paid or unpaid, depending on the employer and arrangement.
An asset purchased with the goal of producing income or growing in value over time. Investments can also lose value.
A debt or other financial obligation that a person or business is responsible for paying.
The smallest amount a lender requires you to pay on a credit account by the due date. Paying only the minimum can increase the time and interest needed to repay a balance.
Using a bank or credit union's mobile app to check balances, deposit checks, transfer money, or pay bills.
Income left after taxes and other deductions. On a paycheck, it is often called take-home pay.
Using a bank or credit union's website to view and manage accounts, transfer money, and pay bills.
When a transaction exceeds the money in an account, the bank may decline it or cover it and charge a fee.
Payment for work that shows gross pay, taxes and other deductions, and the net amount the worker receives.
Digital services used to send money directly to another person. Transfers can be difficult to reverse, so the recipient should be checked before sending.
The original amount borrowed or invested, not including interest. A loan's remaining principal falls as payments reduce the balance.
Insurance that may cover a renter's personal belongings, liability, and certain additional living expenses after a covered loss. It does not insure the building itself.
An individual retirement account funded with after-tax money. Qualified withdrawals are generally tax-free, and contribution rules and limits apply.
A deposit account used to hold money for future needs while earning interest. Rates, fees, and withdrawal rules vary by institution.
Financial aid for education that generally does not have to be repaid, although the award may have eligibility or use requirements.
A dishonest scheme meant to trick people into giving away money or personal information.
Money borrowed to pay eligible education costs. Student loans must be repaid with interest unless a specific discharge, cancellation, or forgiveness program applies.
Required payments to federal, state, or local governments that may be based on income, purchases, property, or other activity.
Costs that can change from month to month, such as groceries, gas, entertainment, or utility use.
A way to separate expenses required for basic living or obligations from optional purchases and experiences.
Money an employer sends from a worker's pay to tax authorities before the worker receives the paycheck.
